rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question means “Have you not been informed/known?”; Ibn Abbas also glosses it as “heard.”
rows.anchor: أي ألم تخبر. وقيل: ألم تعلم. وقال ابن عباس: ألم تسمع؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to the Prophet, the question addresses people generally: the Meccans had seen the event and should recognize the divine favor and believe.
rows.anchor: والخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، ولكنه عام أي ألم تروا ما فعلت بأصحاب الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative wording is rhetorical confirmation, and كيف is accusative as the object of فعل ربك rather than governed by the question’s sense.
rows.anchor: واللفظ استفهام، والمعنى تقرير. والخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fīl is the familiar elephant; the text gives its plural forms and says Ibn al-Sikkit rejects أفيلة, while Sibawayh and al-Akhfash differ over the form فيل.
rows.anchor: والجمع أفيال: وفيول، وفيلة. قال ابن السكيت: ولا تقل أفيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah built the extraordinary Qullays church in Sanaʿa and wrote the Negus that he would redirect the Arabs’ pilgrimage there.
rows.anchor: بنى القليس بصنعاء، وهي كنيسة لم ير مثلها في زمانها بشيء من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An enraged man from the Nasāʾ desecrated the church after hearing Abrahah’s plan, provoking Abrahah to swear he would destroy the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: فخرج حتى أتى الكنيسة، فقعد فيها أي أحدث ثم خرج فلحق بأرضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banu Kinanah killed Abrahah’s envoy sent to summon them to the church pilgrimage, increasing his anger and prompting the Abyssinian expedition.
rows.anchor: فقتلت بنو كنانة ذلك الرجل فزاد أبرهة ذلك غضبا وحنقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab leaders considered defending the sanctuary a duty; Dhu Nafr rallied tribes, fought Abrahah, was defeated and captured, then persuaded Abrahah to spare him.
rows.anchor: فخرج إليه رجل من أشراف أهل اليمن وملوكهم، يقال له ذو نفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nufayl ibn Habib and the Khathʿam tribes fought Abrahah; Nufayl was captured but saved himself by offering to guide the army and secure his tribes’ obedience.
rows.anchor: عرض له نفيل بن حبيب الخثعمي في قبيلتي خثعم: شهران وناهس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Taif, Thaqif claimed its shrine was al-Lat rather than the Kaaba and supplied Abu Righal as a guide; Abu Righal died at al-Mughammas.
rows.anchor: وليس بيتنا هذا البيت الذي تريد يعنون اللات إنما تريد البيت الذي بمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs stoned Abu Righal’s grave at al-Mughammas, a practice recalled in a verse comparing it to stoning his tomb each year.
rows.anchor: فهو القبر الذي يرجم الناس بالمغمس، وفيه يقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah’s cavalry seized the people of Tihama’s property, including two hundred camels belonging to Quraysh leader Abd al-Muttalib.
rows.anchor: وأصاب فيها مائتي بعير لعبد المطلب بن هاشم، وهو يومئذ كبير قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and others considered fighting but abandoned it when they realized they could not match Abrahah’s army.
rows.anchor: فهمت قريش وكنانة وهذيل ومن كان بذلك الحرم بقتاله ثم عرفوا أنهم لا طاقة لهم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah’s envoy told Abd al-Muttalib that the king sought the Kaaba’s destruction, not Quraysh’s blood; Abd al-Muttalib said they could not fight him and trusted the sanctuary’s Lord to protect it.
rows.anchor: هذا بيت الله الحرام، وبيت خليله إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ذو نفر
rows.claim: Dhu Nafr said he could not help as a prisoner but would ask the elephant handler Anis to intercede for Abd al-Muttalib.
rows.anchor: وما غناء رجل أسير بيدي ملك، ينتظر أن يقتله غدوا وعشيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anis presented Abd al-Muttalib as Quraysh’s chief and a generous provider; Abrahah admitted him with honor and seated him beside himself.
rows.anchor: هذا سيد قريش ببابك، يستأذن عليك، وهو صاحب عين مكة

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: Abd al-Muttalib asked Abrahah only to return his two hundred camels; Abrahah reproached him for caring about camels while leaving the Kaaba undefended.
rows.anchor: حاجتي أن يرد علي الملك مائتي بعير أصابها لي

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: Abd al-Muttalib answered that he owned the camels while the House had a Lord who would protect it; Abrahah returned the camels.
rows.anchor: إني أنا رب الإبل، وإن للبيت ربا سيمنعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abd al-Muttalib ordered Quraysh to leave Mecca for mountain ravines, then prayed at the Kaaba’s door with a group of Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وأمرهم بالخروج من مكة والتحرز في شعف الجبال والشعاب

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: In his supplication, Abd al-Muttalib asks God to defend His sanctuary and says the enemy’s cross and strength should not defeat God’s power.
rows.anchor: لا يغلبن صليبهم ومحالهم عدوا محالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥilāl means a plural of ḥill, and al-miḥāl means strength; the poem’s phrase “amrun mā badā laka” means something unprecedented that God might bring about.
rows.anchor: والحلال: جمع حل. والمحال: القوة. وقيل: إن عبد المطلب لما أخذ

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: A second reported prayer asks God alone to protect the Kaaba and identifies the House’s enemy as God’s enemy.
rows.anchor: يا رب لا أرجو لهم سواكا يا رب فامنع منهم حماكا

rows.speaker: عكرمة بن عامر
rows.claim: The poem attributed to ʿIkrima asks God to restrain the raiders and protect the Kaaba, the two hills, and the sacred sites.
rows.anchor: لا هم أخز الأسود بن مقصود الأخذ الهجمة فيها التقليد

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Abd al-Muttalib and Quraysh withdrew to the mountain ravines to await Abrahah’s next move.
rows.anchor: ثم انطلق هو ومن معه من قريش إلى شعف الجبال، فتحرزوا فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah’s elephant was named Mahmud. Nufayl told it to kneel and return from the sanctuary; it refused to advance toward Mecca but walked when pointed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وكان اسم الفيل محمودا، وأبرهة مجمع لهدم البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The birds came from the sea like swallows, each carrying three stones; a strike killed its target, though not every soldier was hit.
rows.anchor: وأرسل الله عليهم طيرا من البحر، أمثال الخطاطيف والبلسان، مع كل طائر منها ثلاثة أحجار

rows.speaker: نفيل بن حبيب
rows.claim: Seeing the punishment, Nufayl taunted the defeated army that there was nowhere to flee from God’s pursuit.
rows.anchor: أين المفر والإله الطالب والأشرم المغلوب ليس الغالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fleeing army collapsed along the roads; Abrahah’s body disintegrated piece by piece, and he died in Sanaʿa after his chest split open.
rows.anchor: وأصيب أبرهة في جسده، وخرجوا به معهم يسقط أنملة أنملة

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل بن سليمان
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil offer a different cause: Quraysh youths accidentally burned a Christian church, enraging the Negus, and Abrahah’s party promised to burn the Kaaba and capture Mecca.
rows.anchor: فتية من قريش خرجوا تجارا إلى أرض النجاشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account identifies the Negus as king, Abrahah as army commander, Abu Yaksum as the king’s companion or minister, and Hajar ibn Shurahbil as a commander.
rows.anchor: وكان النجاشي هو الملك، وأبرهة صاحب الجيش، وأبو يكسوم نديم الملك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies Abu Yaksum as Abrahah ibn al-Sabbah.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: أبو يكسوم هو أبرهة ابن الصباح

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most authorities say the expedition had one elephant, while al-Dahhak says it had eight.
rows.anchor: قال الأكثرون: هو فيل واحد. وقال الضحاك: هي ثمانية فيلة

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Authorities disagree over whether the Negus accompanied the expedition; most say he did not.
rows.anchor: واختلف في النجاشي، هل كان معهم فقال قوم كان معهم. وقال الأكثرون: لم يكن معهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccans described the arriving birds as unfamiliar to the region and compared them to dragonflies; they carried stones in their beaks and feet.
rows.anchor: إن هذه الطير غريبة بأرضنا، وما هي بنجدية ولا تهامية ولا حجازية

rows.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
rows.claim: ʿAta says the birds arrived in the evening, stayed overnight, and stoned the army the next morning.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء بن أبي رباح: جاءت الطير عشية فباتت

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi describes leaders guiding each flock and says each stone bore the name of the person it would kill; another report gives a moral inscription.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: في مناقيرها حصى كحصى الخذف، أمام كل فرقة طائر يقودها

rows.speaker: العوفي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAwfi asked Abu Saʿid al-Khudri about the birds and was told that Mecca’s pigeons descended from them.
rows.anchor: وقال العوفي: سألت عنها أبا سعيد الخدري، فقال: حمام مكة منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A stone could pierce a soldier’s egg, enter his brain, and even pierce an elephant or other beast, disappearing into the earth from impact.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان يقع الحجر على بيضة أحدهم فيخرقها، ويقع في دماغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The army numbered sixty thousand; none returned except its commander and a small band, who later died after recounting what they saw.
rows.anchor: وكان أصحاب الفيل ستين ألفا، لم يرجع منهم أحد إلا أميرهم

rows.speaker: الواقدي
rows.claim: Al-Waqidi says Abrahah al-Ashram was the Negus’s grandfather and was named al-Ashram after Ariat’s spear split his eye, nose, forehead, and lip.
rows.anchor: وقال الواقدي: أبرهة جد النجاشي الذي كان في زمان رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Abrahah’s minister killed Ariat, the Ethiopian army rallied behind Abrahah; he appeased the Negus by sending his shorn hair and soil from his land.
rows.anchor: فجز أبرهة ناصيته وملأ مزودا من تراب أرضه

rows.speaker: قيس بن مخرمة
rows.claim: Qays ibn Makhrama says he and the Prophet were born in the Year of the Elephant.
rows.anchor: وقال قيس بن مخرمة: ولدت أنا ورسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عام الفيل

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi places the Prophet’s birth on Monday, 12 Rabiʿ al-Awwal.
rows.anchor: حكاه الماوردي في التفسير له. وقال في كتاب أعلام النبوة: ولد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يوم الاثنين الثاني عشر من ربيع الأول

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi also transmits a prophetic wording that the Prophet was born on the day of the Elephant.
rows.anchor: وروي عنه أنه قال: " يوم الفيل " حكاه الماوردي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi says the Prophet was born fifty days after the Elephant event; other reports give differing dates and even an eight-month pregnancy.
rows.anchor: وكان بعد الفيل بخمسين يوما

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi rejects as weak the claim that Malik withheld the Prophet’s age to model concealing one’s age; he says a man may disclose whether young or old.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ضعيف لأن مالكا لا يخبر بسن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAttab ibn Asid said the Prophet was older than him, although ʿAttab was senior in age and recalled the elephant’s handler and driver later begging blind.
rows.anchor: ولد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عام الفيل، وأنا أدركت سائسه وقائده أعميين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Elephant event, though before prophethood and the challenge, was a miracle that confirmed and prepared for the Prophet’s mission; many Meccans had witnessed it.
rows.anchor: كانت قصة الفيل فيما بعد من معجزات النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، وإن كانت قبله

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha said she saw the elephant’s blind handler and driver begging people.
rows.anchor: وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها مع حداثة سنها: لقد رأيت قائد الفيل

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih said he saw about two qafiz of the expedition’s stones in Umm Hani’s house, black with red streaks.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح: رأيت في بيت أم هانىء بنت أبي طالب نحوا من قفيزين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God nullified the army’s plot: it meant to kill and enslave Quraysh and demolish the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: أي في إبطال وتضييع لأنهم أرادوا أن يكيدوا قريشا بالقتل والسبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abd Allah, Abd al-Muttalib’s son, found the invaders crushed by the birds and reported their destruction to his father.
rows.anchor: فإذا القوم مشدخين جميعا، فرجع يركض فرسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh reclaimed the army’s wealth; taking its gold and silver further consolidated Abd al-Muttalib’s leadership.
rows.anchor: فأخذوا أموالهم. وكانت أموال بني عبد المطلب منها، وبها تكاملت رياسة عبد المطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Abd al-Muttalib buried two pits of gold and jewels and let his friend Abu Masʿud choose one.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن عبد المطلب حفر حفرتين فملأهما من الذهب والجوهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem thanks God for restraining the Ethiopians and elephants and keeping the battle from reaching Mecca.
rows.anchor: أنت منعت الحبش والأفيالا وقد رعوا بمكة الأجبالا

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the Arabs thereafter honored Quraysh as God’s people, protected by God from the enemy’s burden.
rows.anchor: ولما رد الله الحبشة عن مكة عظمت العرب قريشا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن مخزوم
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmr ibn Makhzum’s poem praises God for immobilizing the elephant at al-Mughammas and leaving the army no escape.
rows.anchor: أنت حبست الفيل بالمغمس من بعد ما هم بشر مبلس

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says these were birds from the sky unlike any seen before or afterward.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: كانت طيرا من السماء لم ير قبلها ولا بعدها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas, transmitted through al-Dahhak, quotes the Prophet describing birds that nest and hatch between heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قال: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the birds as having beaks like bird trunks and hands like dogs’ paws.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: كانت لها خراطيم كخراطيم الطير، وأكف كأكف الكلاب

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the birds were green, sea-born, and lion-headed, unlike anything seen before or later.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: كانت طيرا خضرا، خرجت من البحر، لها رؤوس كرؤوس السباع

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha compares them most closely to swallows; other reports call them bats, green birds with yellow beaks, white birds, or black sea birds.
rows.anchor: وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها: هي أشبه شيء بالخطاطيف

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima glosses أبابيل as gathered flocks; Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say successive groups, while Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Zayd, and al-Akhfash say scattered groups from many directions.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: «أبابيل» أي مجتمعة. وقيل: متتابعة

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says the reported glosses agree in describing large flocks, so the apparent differences are compatible.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وهذه الأقوال متفقة، وحقيقة المعنى: أنها جماعات عظام

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says أبابيل can describe flocks and functions as a plural of abundance without a regular singular; other grammarians offer إبول, إبيل, and إبال.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش يقال: جاءت إبلك أبابيل أي فرقا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says أبابيل has no singular from the same form; al-Ruʾasi heard إبالة, and al-Farra also transmits a lighter form.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: لا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root is associated with accumulation and abundance, with the phrase “he makes much against someone” and the term for gathered camel herds offered as evidence.
rows.anchor: يقال: فلان يؤبل على فلان أي يعظم عليه ويكثر وهو مشتق من الإبل

rows.speaker: رؤبة بن العجاج
rows.claim: Ruʾba’s verse uses أبابيل for the bird flocks that made the defeated army like eaten crop-stalks.
rows.anchor: ولعبت طير بهم أبابيل فصيروا مثل كعصف مأكول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Sihah glosses sijjil as clay stones baked in Hell and inscribed with the people’s names, linking the wording to 51:33–34.
rows.anchor: قالوا: حجارة من طين، طبخت بنار جهنم، مكتوب فيها أسماء القوم

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن أبزى
rows.claim: Ibn Abza says sijjil means stones from heaven, the same stones sent against Lot’s people.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن أبزى: «من سجيل»: من السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation derives sijjil from sijjin by changing n to l, with Ibn Muqbil’s poetic wording cited as evidence.
rows.anchor: وهي «سجين» ثم أبدلت اللام نونا كما قالوا في أصيلان أصيلال

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives sijjil from سجل: the stones were what had been written or decreed for their punishment; the discussion is treated at length under Hud.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: { من سجيل } أي مما كتب عليهم أن يعذبوا به مشتق من السجل

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the stones produced an unprecedented smallpox-like disease when they struck a person.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: كانت ترميهم بحجارة معها، فإذا أصاب أحدهم حجر منها خرج به الجدري

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a stone caused the victim’s skin to blister, and this was the first smallpox.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كان الحجر إذا وقع على أحدهم نفط جلده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has ترميهم with feminine t for the flock; al-Aʿraj and Talha read يرميهم with y, referring to God, as in 8:17, or to the grammatically unmarked birds.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العامة { ترميهم } بالتاء، لتأنيث جماعة الطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the army like crop leaves chewed and discarded by livestock; their severed, scattered limbs resemble fragments of the plant.
rows.anchor: أي جعل الله أصحاب الفيل كورق الزرع إذا أكلته الدواب

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and others transmit the explanation that the simile depicts the army’s body parts scattered like eaten leaves.
rows.anchor: شبه تقطع أوصالهم بتفرق أجزائه. روي معناه عن ابن زيد وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun عصف has forms عصفة, عصافة, and عصيفة; a verse by ʿAlqama supports the meaning “crop leaf.”
rows.anchor: العصف: جمع، واحدته عصفة، وعصافة، وعصيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed kāf in كعصف adds comparison despite the presence of مثل, just as in the wording of 42:11.
rows.anchor: وأدخل الكاف في «كعصف» للتشبيه مع مثل، نحو قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مأكول means that the grain inside has been eaten, like calling someone “handsome” while intending his face.
rows.anchor: ومعنى «مأكول» مأكول حبه. كما يقال: فلان حسن أي حسن وجهه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the simile as wheat husk; a report says stones burst open the victims and left them like a husk stripped of its kernel.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس «فجعلهم كعصف مأكول» أن المراد به قشر البر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud says God sent wind that intensified the stones, making every struck person die; his account includes a Kinda survivor’s poem.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: لما رمت الطير بالحجارة، بعث الله ريحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports say the birds did not strike everyone, while the commander and a small band escaped but died after describing the punishment; Qurtubi leaves the matter to God.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنها لم تصبهم كلهم، لكنها أصابت من شاء الله منهم

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the Arabs thereafter regarded Quraysh as God’s people because God fought the invaders for them.
rows.anchor: لما رد الله الحبشة عن مكة، عظمت العرب قريشا وقالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view connects Surat Quraysh to the Elephant sūra: God destroyed the army so Quraysh could unite, agree, or safely conduct their two trade journeys; Ubayy’s codex had no sūra break.
rows.anchor: قيل: إن هذه السورة متصلة بالتي قبلها في المعنى

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna says an imam he knew recited the two sūras together without separating them.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان بن عيينة: كان لنا إمام لا يفصل بينهما

rows.speaker: عمرو بن ميمون الأودي
rows.claim: ʿAmr ibn Maymun reports that ʿUmar recited al-Tin first and then al-Fil and Quraysh in the next rakʿa.
rows.anchor: صلينا المغرب خلف عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه فقرأ في الأولى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the previous sūra recalled God’s favor in destroying the invaders: Quraysh’s caravans had traveled unmolested because they were sanctuary people.
rows.anchor: أي فعلنا ذلك بأصحاب الفيل نعمة منا على قريش

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ibn Abbas, in a report through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, explain the act as enabling Quraysh to travel safely and become accustomed to their journeys.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول مجاهد وابن عباس في رواية سعيد بن جبير عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God’s favor was Quraysh’s winter and summer journeys; they wintered in Mecca and summered in Taif.
rows.anchor: قال: نعمتي على قريش إيلافهم رحلة الشتاء والصيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative view separates the sūras because the basmala marks a new opening and attaches the lām of لإيلاف to فليعبدوا in the following verse.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ليست بمتصلة لأن بين السورتين «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم»

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil also treats the sūras as separate, construing the sense as God made Quraysh accustomed, so they should worship the House’s Lord.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال الخليل: ليست متصلة كأنه قال: ألف الله قريشا إيلافا

rows.speaker: الكسائي والأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi and al-Akhfash say the lām can express wonder: “Marvel at Quraysh’s habituation.” Another view gives it the sense of إلى.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اللام في قوله تعالى: { لإيلاف قريش } لام التعجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings include Ibn ʿAmir’s hamzated form without yāʾ, and Abu Jaʿfar and al-Aʿraj’s shortened form without hamza; others read the fully hamzated form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر: «لإئلاف قريش» مهموزا مختلسا بلا ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment cites poetry supporting forms of īlāf and describes the different readings, including Abu Jaʿfar’s لإلف and ʿIkrima’s imperative ليألف in Ibn Masʿud’s codex.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر أيضا: «لإلف قريش» وقد جمعهما من قال

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima read ليألف as an imperative with an open lām and criticized the reading لإيلاف.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة «ليألف» بفتح اللام على الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana; a competing definition limits the name to descendants of Fihr, but Qurtubi says the Nadr lineage is sounder.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن قريشا بنو فهر بن مالك بن النضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report says the Prophet’s clan are descendants of al-Nadr, neither disowning their father nor attributing themselves to their mother.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال

rows.speaker: وائلة بن الأسقع
rows.claim: Waʾila ibn al-Asqaʿ transmits the hadith that God selected Kinanah, Quraysh, Banu Hashim, and finally the Prophet from successive descendants of Ishmael.
rows.anchor: وقال وائلة بن الأسقع: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi calls the lineage report about al-Nadr sound and established, and says al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted it.
rows.anchor: صحيح ثابت، خرجه البخاري ومسلم وغيرهما

rows.speaker: أبو جلدة اليشكري
rows.claim: Abu Jilda al-Yashkuri’s verse supports the etymology connecting Quraysh with gathering and cohesion.
rows.anchor: قال أبو جلدة اليشكري: إخوة قرشوا الذنوب علينا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra supports deriving Quraysh from trade and acquisition, since they earned and accumulated wealth.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وبه سميت قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation connects their name to searching pilgrims for those in need and meeting their needs; poetry supports this derivation.
rows.anchor: لأنهم كانوا يفتشون الحاج من ذي الخلة، فيسدون خلته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The sea-creature explanation is elaborated by Ibn Abbas’s comparison of Quraysh to a dominant fish, with verses attributed to Tubbaʿ.
rows.anchor: لدابة في البحر من أقوى دوابه يقال لها القرش تأكل ولا تؤكل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and others report readings إلفهم without yāʾ, including a version heard by Asmaʾ from the Prophet; other readers vary the hamza and length.
rows.anchor: قرأ مجاهد وحميد «إلفهم» ساكنة اللام بغير ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority reading إيلافهم is preferred and treated as an explanatory substitute for the first إيلاف, meaning what Quraysh had become accustomed to.
rows.anchor: الباقون «إيلافهم» بالمد والهمز وهو الاختيار، وهو بدل من الإيلاف الأول للبيان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the winter and summer journeys were made easy for Quraysh as a divine favor.
rows.anchor: روى ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Harawi and others say the four sons of Abd Manaf secured travel agreements with regional rulers, protecting Quraysh caravans to Syria, Abyssinia, Yemen, and Persia.
rows.anchor: وكان أصحاب الإيلاف أربعة إخوة: هاشم، وعبد شمس، والمطلب، ونوفل بنو عبد مناف

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari explains īlāf as granting safe-conduct or protection; Quraysh had no farming or livestock and imported supplies safely while surrounding people were raided.
rows.anchor: الإيلاف: شبه الإجارة بالخفارة يقال: آلف يؤلف: إذا أجار الحمائل بالخفارة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes earlier famine custom: a person and family withdrew to a known tent to die one by one until ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Manaf’s household intervened.
rows.anchor: في قول الله عز وجل: { لإيلاف قريش } إلفهم رحلة الشتاء والصيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Faris notes uncertainty about the transmitted word يعتفد, wondering whether it means going to die in the tent, but does not know its exact sense.
rows.anchor: قال ابن فارس: هذه لفظة في هذا الخبر لا أدري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the starving boy again warned that his family would die, ʿAmr outlawed the death-tent custom, organized relief, slaughtered animals, and fed the people, earning the name Hashim.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه نحر البدن، وذبح الكباش والمعز، ثم هشم الثريد، وأطعم الناس فسمي هاشما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hashim organized winter journeys to Yemen and summer journeys to Syria; prosperous Quraysh shared profits until the poor and rich were nearly equal.
rows.anchor: ثم جمع كل بني أب على رحلتين: في الشتاء إلى اليمن، وفي الصيف إلى الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage interprets the command to worship as a response to Hashim’s provisioning and the protection that kept Quraysh from being outnumbered and subdued.
rows.anchor: فقال: { ليعبدوا رب هذا البيت الذي أطعمهم من جوع } بصنيع هاشم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رحلة is accusative as a verbal noun for their journey, as the object of إيلافهم, or as an adverbial; nominative is possible, but Qurtubi prefers the first analysis.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { رحلة الشتآء والصيف } «رحلة» نصب بالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The winter route went to warmer Yemen and the summer route to cooler Syria; Ibn Abbas also says Quraysh wintered in warm Mecca and summered in Taif.
rows.anchor: وكانت إحدى الرحلتين إلى اليمن في الشتاء، لأنها بلاد حامية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrasting warm and cool places were a major blessing, protecting Quraysh from winter cold and summer heat.
rows.anchor: وهذه من أجل النعم أن يكون للقوم ناحية حر تدفع عنهم برد الشتاء

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi links لإيلاف to the preceding sūra and says reciters may stop before a complete sentence to teach meanings; stop when breath runs out, then resume where breath stopped.
rows.anchor: اختار القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي وغيره من العلماء: أن قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says he sees no evidence for Ibn al-ʿArabi’s claim, but personally follows stops at complete meanings out of deference to earlier authorities.
rows.anchor: ولا دليل على ما قالوه بحال، ولكني أعتمد الوقف على التمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s pauses after verses of al-Fatiha and the consensus that stopping at كعصف مأكول is acceptable support stopping at every verse ending.
rows.anchor: ومن الدليل على صحة هذا، قراءة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم { الحمد لله رب العالمين } ثم يقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse endings beautify ordered speech; pausing at them displays that beauty, while omitting pauses hides it and makes verse resemble prose.
rows.anchor: فإن الفواصل حلية وزينة للكلام المنظوم

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik divides the year into equal winter and summer halves; Rabiʿa and his companions treated the Pleiades’ rising as summer’s start and winter’s end.
rows.anchor: قال مالك: الشتاء نصف السنة، والصيف نصفها، ولم أزل أرى ربيعة بن أبي عبد الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s two journeys support arranging daily life for seasonal comfort, such as using a cooler seaside room in summer and warmer southern room in winter.
rows.anchor: كان فيه دليل على جواز تصرف الرجل في الزمانين بين محلين

rows.speaker: أشهب
rows.claim: Ashhab alone reports a different seasonal marker: when al-Haqʿa sets, the night shortens.
rows.anchor: وقال عنه أشهب وحده: إذا سقطت الهقعة نقص الليل

rows.speaker: محمد بن عبد الحكم
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam says a winter-bound oath lasts until 17 Hator and a summer-bound oath until 17 Bashans.
rows.anchor: وقد سئل محمد بن عبد الحكم عمن حلف ألا يكلم امرأ

rows.speaker: القرظي
rows.claim: Al-Qurazi corrects the summer date in Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam’s ruling from 17 to 19 Bashans.
rows.anchor: قال القرظي: أما ذكر هذا عن محمد في بشنس، فهو سهو، إنما هو تسعة عشر من بشنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers Malik’s two-part division over the reported four-season divisions because the verse divides time into two halves.
rows.anchor: والذي قاله مالك أصح لأن الله قسم الزمان قسمين ولم يجعل لهما ثالثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command requires worship and exclusive devotion to God in gratitude for the two journeys; if other favors do not move them, this clear favor should.
rows.anchor: أمرهم الله تعالى بعبادته وتوحيده، لأجل إيلافهم رحلتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed fāʾ reflects conditional reasoning: if they will not worship for other blessings, they should worship for this manifest one.
rows.anchor: ودخلت الفاء لأجل ما في الكلام من معنى الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the Lord of this House distinguishes Him from Quraysh’s idols; alternatively, it recalls that the Kaaba gave Quraysh status among Arabs.
rows.anchor: وفي تعريف نفسه لهم بأنه رب هذا البيت وجهان

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the command asks Quraysh to become accustomed to worshipping the Kaaba’s Lord as they had become accustomed to the two journeys.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { فليعبدوا رب هذا البيت } أي ليألفوا عبادة رب الكعبة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says Quraysh traveled to Busra and Yemen and were told instead to remain in Mecca; winter journey went to Yemen, summer to Syria.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: كانت قريش قد ألفوا رحلة إلى بصرى ورحلة إلى اليمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fed Quraysh after hunger; Ibn Abbas connects their security to Abraham’s prayer for a safe city and provision, while Ibn Zayd cites the sanctuary’s protection from tribal raids.
rows.anchor: { الذي أطعمهم من جوع } أي بعد جوع. { وآمنهم من خوف } قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Quraysh were protected from the raids and captivity common among Arabs because they lived in the sanctuary, as supported by 28:57.
rows.anchor: كانت العرب يغير بعضها على بعض، ويسبى بعضها من بعض، فأمنت قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says hardship on the two journeys led God to inspire Abyssinians to bring food by ship; Quraysh feared an invasion but were relieved by the food.
rows.anchor: فألقى الله في قلوب الحبشة أن يحملوا إليهم طعاما في السفن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says after Quraysh rejected Muhammad, his prayer brought famine; they asked him to pray, then food arrived from fertile Tabaala and Jarash.
rows.anchor: اللهم اجعلها عليهم سنين كسنى يوسف

rows.speaker: الضحاك والربيع وشريك وسفيان
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak, al-Rabiʿ, Sharik, and Sufyan interpret “fear” as protection from leprosy.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك والربيع وشريك وسفيان

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash interprets Quraysh’s security as protection from the Abyssinians with the elephant.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعمش: { وآمنهم من خوف } أي من خوف الحبشة مع الفيل

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAli interprets the security as assurance that the caliphate would remain among Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وقال على رضى الله عنه: وآمنهم من خوف: أن تكون الخلافة إلا فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is that the safe-conduct from rulers spared Quraysh from paying for protection; Qurtubi concludes that the wording encompasses all these meanings.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أى كفاهم أخذ الإيلاف من الملوك. فالله أعلم، واللفظ يعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religion here means requital and the accounting of the afterlife; the question omits its answer, asking whether the denier is right or mistaken.
rows.anchor: أي بالجزاء والحساب في الآخرة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains that the second hamza in أرأيت remains because the verb is not contracted to ريت; the interrogative hamza is softened to an alif.
rows.anchor: و { أرأيت } بإثبات الهمزة الثانية إذ لا يقال في أرأيت: ريت

rows.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Abu Salih transmits from Ibn Abbas that the sūra was revealed about al-ʿAs ibn Waʾil; al-Kalbi and Muqatil agree.
rows.anchor: نزلت في العاص بن وائل السهمي

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas’s alternative view that it concerned one of the hypocrites.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عنه قال: نزلت في رجل من المنافقين

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the revelation concerned al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; other opinions name Abu Jahl or ʿAmr ibn ʿAʾidh.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the sūra was revealed about Abu Sufyan, who struck an orphan with his staff after the child asked him for something.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج: نزلت في أبي سفيان، وكان ينحر في كل أسبوع جزورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: يدع means to push away; Ibn Abbas says the denier pushes an orphan away from his due, while Qatada says he subjugates and wrongs the child.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك عن ابن عباس. { فذلك الذي يدع اليتيم } أي يدفعه عن حقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recalls that pre-Islamic Arabs denied inheritance to women and children, claiming only warriors deserved property.
rows.anchor: أنهم كانوا لا يورثون النساء ولا الصغار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report promises Paradise for the Muslim who cares for an orphan until the child becomes self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: من ضم يتيما من المسلمين حتى يستغني، فقد وجبت له الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not urging people to feed the poor reflects stinginess and denial of requital; the same wording occurs at 69:34.
rows.anchor: وهو مثل قوله تعالى في سورة الحاقة: ولا يحض على طعام المسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke does not include those unable to feed; it targets people who excuse withholding by saying God could feed the poor, as in 36:47.
rows.anchor: أنطعم من لو يشآء الله أطعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woe announced for the worshippers means punishment.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { فويل للمصلين } أي عذاب لهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas’s view that the heedless worshipper expects no reward for prayer and fears no punishment for abandoning it.
rows.anchor: فروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال: هو المصلي الذي إن صلى لم يرج لها ثوابا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas identifies heedlessness as delaying prayers beyond their appointed times.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا: الذين يؤخرونها عن أوقاتها

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim says the phrase means wasting prayer time; Abu al-ʿAliya adds failing to pray on time or complete bowing and prostration.
rows.anchor: وكذا روى المغيرة عن إبراهيم، قال: ساهون بإضاعة الوقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The neglected prayer is linked to the later generation that squandered prayer at 19:59.
rows.anchor: فخلف من بعدهم خلف أضاعوا الصلاة

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim also says the heedless person turns his head while rising from prostration.
rows.anchor: وروي عن إبراهيم أيضا: أنه الذي إذا سجد قام برأسه هكذا ملتفتا

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub defines heedlessness as failing to recite or remember God.
rows.anchor: وقال قطرب: هو ألا يقرأ ولا يذكر الله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud’s reading has لاهون, “distracted,” instead of the common ساهون.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة عبد الله «الذين هم عن صلاتهم لاهون»

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص
rows.claim: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas transmits the Prophet’s explanation that they negligently postpone prayer beyond its time.
rows.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله: { فويل للمصلين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verses describe hypocrites who leave prayer privately but perform it publicly, matching 4:142; Malik reports the same interpretation.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: هم المنافقون يتركون الصلاة سرا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that had the verse said “in their prayer,” it would have referred to believers’ involuntary distraction rather than neglect of prayer.
rows.anchor: ولو قال في صلاتهم ساهون لكانت في المؤمنين

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAta praises the wording عن صلاتهم because it says they neglect prayer itself, not that distraction happens within prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: الحمد لله الذي قال: «عن صلاتهم» ولم يقل في صلاتهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes neglecting prayer (عن) from distraction during prayer (في), which may happen to any Muslim through Satan or inner thoughts.
rows.anchor: معنى «عن» أنهم ساهون عنها سهو ترك لها وقلة التفات إليها

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi says freedom from in-prayer forgetfulness is impossible; someone who never lapses may not ponder the prayer, while the Prophet could be distracted by weightier matters.
rows.anchor: لأن السلامة من السهو محال، وقد سها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في صلاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Showing worship to people while claiming devotion is ostentation; its true aim is worldly gain and status in people’s hearts.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة الرياء طلب ما في الدنيا بالعبادة، وأصله طلب المنزلة في قلوب الناس

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi lists ostentation through appearance, coarse clothing, public speech, and displaying or beautifying prayer and charity to be seen.
rows.anchor: وأولها تحسين السمت وهو من أجزاء النبوة، ويريد بذلك الجاه والثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Publicly displaying a required good deed is not ostentation, because obligatory acts properly may be announced and made visible.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون الرجل مرائيا بإظهار العمل الصالح إن كان فريضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading is أعطيناك; al-Hasan and Talha read أنطيناك, also reported from the Prophet by Umm Salama, as an Arabic synonym for giving.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وطلحة بن مصرف: «أنطيناك» بالنون وروته أم سلمة عن النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawthar is an intensive form derived from abundance; Arabic uses it for anything great or plentiful, including wealth, a generous leader, followers, and dust.
rows.anchor: فوعل من الكثرة مثل النوفل من النفل

rows.speaker: الكميت
rows.claim: Al-Kumayt’s verse calls Marwan’s father a kawthar, meaning a leader rich in goodness.
rows.anchor: وكان أبوك ابن العقائل كوثرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first reported interpretation is a river in Paradise, transmitted from Anas by al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi.
rows.anchor: الأول: أنه نهر في الجنة رواه البخاري عن أنس

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar transmits the Prophet’s description of a Paradise river with golden banks, jeweled bed, fragrant earth, and water sweeter than honey.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi labels Ibn ʿUmar’s river report hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: هذا حديث حسن صحيح

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAta’s second interpretation is the Prophet’s pool at the gathering place on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أنه حوض النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في الموقف قاله عطاء

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: In Anas’s Sahih Muslim report, the Prophet calls Kawthar a river promised by God, whose abundant goodness includes a pool for his community, with vessels as numerous as stars.
rows.anchor: قال: «فإنه نهر وعدنيه ربي عز وجل، عليه خير كثير هو حوض ترد عليه أمتي

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: The report says some people are pulled away from the pool; when the Prophet says they are his community, he is told he does not know what they changed after him.
rows.anchor: فيختلج العبد منهم فأقول إنه من أمتي، فيقال إنك لا تدري ما أحدث بعدك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports about the pool are numerous; Qurtubi says the four rightly guided caliphs stand at its corners and refers readers to his book on the subject.
rows.anchor: والأخبار في حوضه في الموقف كثيرة، ذكرناها في كتاب «التذكرة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The river or pool may be called Kawthar because many people drink from it and because it contains abundant goodness and water.
rows.anchor: ثم يجوز أن يسمى ذلك النهر أو الحوض كوثرا، لكثرة الواردة والشاربة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Other interpretations identify Kawthar as prophethood and scripture, according to ʿIkrima.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أن الكوثر النبوة والكتاب قاله عكرمة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets Kawthar as the Qurʾan; al-Mughira says Islam and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl says ease in reciting Qurʾan and lighter laws.
rows.anchor: الرابع: القرآن قاله الحسن. الخامس: الإسلام حكاه المغيرة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن عياش ويمان بن رئاب
rows.claim: Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash and Yaman ibn Riʾab say Kawthar means the Prophet’s many companions, community, and followers.
rows.anchor: هو كثرة الأصحاب والأمة والأشياع قاله أبو بكر بن عياش

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan interprets Kawthar as preferring others over oneself; al-Mawardi offers renown, and another report says it is light in the heart.
rows.anchor: الثامن: أنه الإيثار قاله ابن كيسان

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabi transmits that Kawthar means divine miracles guiding those who answer the Prophet’s call; other views include intercession, testimony of faith, and religious understanding.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معجزات الرب هدي بها أهل الإجابة لدعوتك حكاه الثعلبي

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Kawthar means something great, citing Labid’s poetry.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: هو العظيم من الأمر وذكر بيت لبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says the strongest interpretations are the Paradise river and the Prophet’s pool, because explicit sound reports establish them; the other blessings may also have been granted in addition.
rows.anchor: أصح هذه الأقوال الأول والثاني لأنه ثابت عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم نص في الكوثر

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas said elderly women prayed for water from the Prophet’s pool, rejecting people’s doubts about its reality.
rows.anchor: ما كنت أرى أن أعيش حتى أرى أمثالكم يتمارون في الحوض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas’s view that فصل commands the Prophet to perform his obligatory prayer.
rows.anchor: أي أقم الصلاة المفروضة عليك كذا رواه الضحاك عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة وعطاء وعكرمة
rows.claim: Qatada, ʿAta, and ʿIkrima interpret فصل as the Eid prayer on the Day of Sacrifice and انحر as sacrificing an animal.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وعطاء وعكرمة: «فصل لربك» صلاة العيد يوم النحر

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas says the Prophet slaughtered before praying, so he was commanded to pray first and then sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وقال أنس: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ينحر ثم يصلي

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says the command means the dawn prayer at Muzdalifa and sacrificing camels at Mina.
rows.anchor: صل لربك صلاة الصبح المفروضة بجمع، وانحر البدن بمنى

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr also links the verse to Hudaybiyya, where the confined Prophet was told to pray, sacrifice, and depart, which he did.
rows.anchor: نزلت في الحديبية حين حصر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن البيت

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi argues for the five obligatory prayers because they are Islam’s foundation; the Muzdalifa interpretation singles out dawn because it precedes sacrifice that day.
rows.anchor: أما من قال: إن المراد بقوله تعالى: { فصل } الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says the Eid-prayer interpretation cannot apply in Mecca, where Ibn ʿUmar reports there is no Eid prayer by consensus.
rows.anchor: وأما من قال إنها صلاة العيد فذلك بغير مكة إذ ليس بمكة صلاة عيد بإجماع

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says he heard no transmitted explanation but personally takes the command as prayer on the Day of Sacrifice followed by sacrifice.
rows.anchor: فأما مالك فقال: ما سمعت فيه شيئا، والذي يقع في نفسي أن المراد

rows.speaker: علي ومحمد بن كعب
rows.claim: ʿAli and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb interpret the command as placing the right hand over the left at the chest during prayer; Ibn Abbas is also cited.
rows.anchor: وقال علي رضي الله عنه ومحمد بن كعب: المعنى ضع اليمنى على اليسرى

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Another report from ʿAli interprets وانحر as raising the hands to the chest when saying the opening takbir.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي أيضا: أن يرفع يديه في التكبير إلى نحره

rows.speaker: جعفر بن علي
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn ʿAli says the hands are raised at the opening takbir; a report from ʿAli also includes rising from bowing and prostrating.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال جعفر بن علي: { فصل لربك وانحر } قال: يرفع يديه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In a report from ʿAli, Gabriel tells the Prophet that نحر is not slaughter but raising the hands at takbir, rising from bowing, and prostration, as prayer’s adornment.
rows.anchor: ليست بنحيرة، ولكنه يأمرك إذا تحرمت للصلاة، أن ترفع يديك إذا كبرت
